newsitem.title: USA: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-SUPER BOWL IN NEW ORLEANS A DREAM FOR FAVRE.
newsitem.headline: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-SUPER BOWL IN NEW ORLEANS A DREAM FOR FAVRE.

text.p: After a nightmarish off-season, Green Bay Packers star quarterback Brett Favre is living a post-season dream.
"I did dream of being here and I hoped that I would be here. I worked very hard to get here so I'm pretty excited," Favre said Tuesday at the pre-Super Bowl circus known as media day.

Sporting sunglasses indoors in the Louisiana Superdome, courtesy of Green Bay's outrageous backup quarterback Jim McMahon, Favre appeared surprisingly comfortable in his first full tilt scrimmage with the media masses.

"It's a little crazy, I guess. But we've earned the right to be here and that's part of it so we'll just kind of go with the flow," said Favre, who will lead his team against the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XXXI on Sunday.

But last May when Favre revealed his addiction to the painkiller Vicodin and checked himself into a rehabilition clinic for more than six weeks, few thought he would be taking centre stage at the NFL's big show the very next season.

That is, few besides Favre himself, who emerged from rehab in July and had the audacity to proclaim that he was Super Bowl bound, saying: "All I can tell people is if they don't believe me, just bet against me."

He then backed up his claim with a brilliant season, playing through pain and injuries without missing a game before being named the league's Most Valuable Player for the second successive season -- a feat only previously accomplished by the legendary Joe Montana.

The 27-year-old Favre led the league with 39 touchdown passes -- third best in NFL history -- completed nearly 60 percent of his passes for 3,899 yards, had five games with four touchdowns, and threw just 13 interceptions in a league-best 13-3 regular season.
Green Bay coach Mike Holmgren has little doubt that his resiliant star can withstand the over-hyped madness of Super Bowl week.

"After all the stuff he has gone through in a year, I'm not going to say the Super Bowl is overwhelming to him because he has had to battle some things way more serious than he is going through this week and he has come through it well," Holmgren said.

"As you're going through tough times, you're mad, you're sad, you're angry and all of that," Favre recalled. "But then when you're in a position like this and you're in the Super Bowl, you appreciate it."

Making the experience all the more special is that the big game is taking place just about 60 miles (95 km) from the tiny Mississippi town of Kiln, where Favre grew up sharing swimming holes with alligators and where his parents still reside.

"It's a little wild there," he said of the Packers mania that has swept Kiln. "They have something to do right now. Usually this time of year, we're boiling crawfish ... we're not worried about the Super Bowl.
"But they have a chance to watch this game and pull for someone they know. People there are really excited and I'm as happy for them as they are proud of me."

Favre also feels right at home in the Superdome, where he as never lost as a college player with Southern Mississippi against Tulane, or as a pro with Atlanta and Green Bay against the New Orleans Saints.
"I'm excited to play here. It's a fun place to play and I want to do well in front of the people here at home," added Favre, who had to get 40 tickets for family and friends.
Favre said McMahon, the league's former wild child who led the Chicago Bears to a Super Bowl title 11 years ago in New Orleans, gave the team some pointers on dealing with the NFL extravaganza.
"Whatever Jim says, you just do totally the opposite," Favre joked.
"We feel like we belong here. It's everything we hoped it would be. Now, we just hope we can go out and win this ballgame on Sunday."
